hints: Count outer shell electrons for each atom first: S has 6, O has 6, each Cl has 7. Remember S can expand its octet and here forms four bonds.
Think about how many lone pairs remain on each terminal atom after bonding: O in S=O keeps two lone pairs, each Cl keeps three lone pairs, and S keeps one lone pair.
walkthrough:
Set up the skeleton and electron count**
Picture S in the middle with O and two Cl atoms around it. S is in Period 3 so it can hold more than 8 electrons. Here it makes four bonds in total, one double bond to O ($\text{S=O}$ counts as two) plus two single bonds to Cl. That uses 4 shared pairs.

Add the lone pairs to complete octets**
Now finish every atom. O already shares 2 pairs, so give it 2 lone pairs to reach 8. Each Cl shares 1 pair, so give each Cl 3 lone pairs. S has 4 shared pairs (8 electrons) plus one extra lone pair of its own. In total you should have 9 lone pairs drawn with dots and crosses for outer shell only.

Final answer: Dot-and-cross diagram showing S central bonded to O by double bond ($\text{S=O}$) and to two Cl by single bonds ($2 \times \text{S-Cl}$).
All 9 lone pairs shown: 2 pairs on O, 3 pairs on each Cl, 1 pair on S.

hints: Recall that $\text{HCl}$ is a strong monoprotic acid, so it reacts with $\text{NaOH}$ in a 1:1 ratio to give a chloride salt and water.
Recall that $\text{SO}_{2}$ is an acidic oxide and with excess concentrated $\text{NaOH}$ it forms the normal sulfite salt plus water, needing 2 moles of $\text{NaOH}$ per mole of $\text{SO}_{2}$.
walkthrough:
Neutralisation of HCl**
$\text{HCl}$ is a simple strong acid. One $\text{OH}^{-}$ neutralises one $\text{H}^{+}$: $$\text{NaOH} + \text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{NaCl} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$

Absorption of SO2**
$\text{SO}_{2}$ dissolves to give sulfurous acid, which is diprotic. With excess $\text{NaOH}$ both protons are neutralised to give sodium sulfite: $$2\text{NaOH} + \text{SO}_{2} \rightarrow \text{Na}_{2}\text{SO}_{3} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$ This 2:1 ratio is vital for the next calculation.

Final answer: $\text{NaOH} + \text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{NaCl} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$
$2\text{NaOH} + \text{SO}_{2} \rightarrow \text{Na}_{2}\text{SO}_{3} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

hints: Start by calculating initial moles of $\text{NaOH}$ from $60.0 \text{ cm}^{3}$ of $0.500 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ solution, then calculate leftover moles from the $10.8 \text{ cm}^{3}$ titration.
Subtract leftover moles from initial moles to find moles that reacted with the acidic gases.
walkthrough:
Find initial and excess NaOH**
Use $n = cV$ with $V$ in $\text{dm}^{3}$ (divide $\text{cm}^{3}$ by 1000). Initial: $$n = 0.500 \times \frac{60.0}{1000} = 3.00 \times 10^{-2} \text{ mol}$$ Leftover titrated by $\text{H}^{+}$ in 1:1 ratio: $$n = 0.500 \times \frac{10.8}{1000} = 5.40 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$$

Back titrate to get reacted moles**
The $\text{NaOH}$ that disappeared was used up by $\text{SO}_{2}$ and $\text{HCl}$: $$n(\text{reacted}) = 3.00 \times 10^{-2} - 5.40 \times 10^{-3} = 2.46 \times 10^{-2} \text{ mol}$$

Final answer: Initial moles $\text{NaOH} = 0.500 \times 60.0/1000 = 3.00 \times 10^{-2} \text{ mol}$
Leftover moles $\text{NaOH} = 0.500 \times 10.8/1000 = 5.40 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$
Moles reacted $= 3.00 \times 10^{-2} - 5.40 \times 10^{-3} = 2.46 \times 10^{-2} \text{ mol}$

hints: From (b)(i), 1 mole of $\text{RCO}_{2}\text{H}$ gives 1 mole $\text{HCl}$ needing 1 mole $\text{NaOH}$ plus 1 mole $\text{SO}_{2}$ needing 2 moles $\text{NaOH}$, so find total $\text{NaOH}$ per mole of acid.
walkthrough:
Link NaOH back to carboxylic acid**
Look at the two equations together. One $\text{RCO}_{2}\text{H}$ produces one $\text{HCl}$ and one $\text{SO}_{2}$. From part (i): $\text{HCl}$ uses $1 \times \text{NaOH}$, $\text{SO}_{2}$ uses $2 \times \text{NaOH}$. So total $= 3$ moles $\text{NaOH}$ per mole of acid. Therefore: $$n(\text{RCO}_{2}\text{H}) = \frac{2.46 \times 10^{-2}}{3} = 8.20 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$$
Final answer: Moles of $\text{RCO}_{2}\text{H} = 2.46 \times 10^{-2} / 3 = 8.20 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$

hints: Use $M_{r} = mass / moles$ with mass $1.00 \text{ g}$ and your answer from (b)(iii).
walkthrough:
Calculate Mr directly**
Relative molecular mass is mass of one mole: $$M_{r} = \frac{m}{n} = \frac{1.00}{8.20 \times 10^{-3}} = 122$$ No units for $M_{r}$, and this value points to a familiar acid.

hints: Subtract the mass of the $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ group ($M = 45$) from $M_{r} = 122$ to find the mass left for R, then fit C and H only to that mass.
walkthrough:
Work out R then the full formula**
$\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ has mass $12 + 32 + 1 = 45$. So mass of R $= 122 - 45 = 77$. With C and H only, $77 = (6 \times 12) + 5$, so R $= \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}$. Add back $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$: $$\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CO}_{2}\text{H} = \text{C}_{7}\text{H}_{6}\text{O}_{2}$$ This is benzoic acid.
Final answer: $\text{C}_{7}\text{H}_{6}\text{O}_{2}$

hints: Identify the functional group change in step 3: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CONH}_{2}$ (amide) to $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$ (amine), so think which powerful hydride reduces amides.
walkthrough:
Spot amide to amine reduction**
Step 3 converts $\text{C=O}$ in the amide $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CONH}_{2}$ to $\text{CH}_{2}$ in the amine $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$. This needs the strong reducing agent lithium aluminium hydride, $\text{LiAlH}_{4}$. $\text{NaBH}_{4}$ is too weak for amides.

hints: Use the last clue first: U is a primary amine made from 1-bromo-2-methylbutane plus ammonia, so draw that carbon skeleton with $\text{NH}_{2}$ replacing Br.
Work backwards: U comes from reduction of an amide, which comes from T (a carboxylic acid), so T has the same skeleton as U but with $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ in place of $\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$.
Angelic acid becomes T by adding $\text{H}_{2}$ across a C=C bond, so introduce a double bond into the T skeleton while keeping formula $\text{C}_{5}\text{H}_{8}\text{O}_{2}$.
walkthrough:
Deduce U from the bromoalkane**
1-bromo-2-methylbutane is $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}(\text{CH}_{3})\text{CH}_{2}\text{Br}$. Reaction with excess ammonia is nucleophilic substitution of Br by $\text{NH}_{2}$, giving U as $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}(\text{CH}_{3})\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$ (2-methylbutan-1-amine). Formula checks as $\text{C}_{5}\text{H}_{13}\text{N}$.

Deduce T from the synthetic route**
The route is acid to acyl chloride to amide to amine with no change in carbon skeleton except $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ becomes $\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$. So reverse it: replace $\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$ in U by $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ to get T as $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}(\text{CH}_{3})\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ (2-methylbutanoic acid, $\text{C}_{5}\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_{2}$).

Deduce angelic acid by dehydrogenation**
Angelic acid $\text{C}_{5}\text{H}_{8}\text{O}_{2}$ gives T on hydrogenation with $\text{H}_{2}$ plus Ni, so it is the alkene version: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}=\text{C}(\text{CH}_{3})\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ (2-methylbut-2-enoic acid). This fits addition of $\text{H}_{2}$ across the double bond.

Final answer: angelic acid: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}=\text{C}(\text{CH}_{3})\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$
T: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}(\text{CH}_{3})\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$
U: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}(\text{CH}_{3})\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$

hints: Check for a C=C with two different groups on each carbon for angelic acid, and for a carbon with four different groups in T.
walkthrough:
Assign the stereoisomerism type**
Angelic acid has $\text{C=C}$ with different substituents on each carbon ($\text{CH}_{3}$ and H on one end, $\text{CH}_{3}$ and $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ on the other), so it shows geometrical or cis-trans isomerism. T has a chiral centre at C2 bonded to H, $\text{CH}_{3}$, $\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ and $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$, so it shows optical isomerism.

Final answer: angelic acid: geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism
compound T: optical isomerism
